# Timing

> "Behold, now is the acceptable time. Behold, now is the day of salvation."
>
> — 2 Corinthians 6:2

The habit is doing you no good, so the right time to stop is now. Even so, timing deserves some thought.

For many men, getting caught by this at thirteen was the worst thing that ever happened to them, and they've never told anyone. Something like that deserves to be dealt with properly, and that includes when.

## Your schedule {-}

In this book the "when" is simple. If you're ready today, today is the day. At the latest, you stop at the final step, near the end of the book. That is what stopping right away means. There's no tapering and no ninety-day climb. So you're not choosing a date so much as getting ready for one.

## Before the day {-}

There are two things to look at before that day comes. First, work out when the habit seems to matter most to you. If it's your pressure valve, the worst week at work will look like the wrong week. If it's your cure for boredom, the long empty vacation will. Know which kind you are, because that's where the Big Monster will try to bargain.

Next, look at the three weeks after you expect to finish. Is there a trip away on your own? Is your partner visiting her mother? Is there a woman you already know you shouldn't see? Are there finals, a deadline, a string of late nights in an empty house? None of these has to put you off. They only need to be seen coming. A man who expects the quiet hotel room, and knows he's missing nothing in it, walks straight through it.

In the meantime, don't cut down. Cutting down only teaches you that being denied makes it precious. Make one change: pay attention. If you fall while you're reading, notice how it starts without your deciding. Notice the hunt, how short the end is and how flat the ten minutes after it are. Notice that nothing you were promised turned up. You're not looking for disgust. You're looking for the truth, and you've never watched before.

## The week that never comes {-}

**Whatever you do, don't tell yourself "not now, later" and put the book in a drawer.** Keep reading, know roughly when you'll finish, and look forward to that day.

Remember that you aren't giving anything up. You're about to be handed a great deal.

Here is the cleverest twist in the trap. When life is stressful, it's the wrong time to stop, because you "need" it. When life is calm, you feel no urgency, because things aren't so bad. One or the other is always true, so the right time never comes. Notice that it is never a bad week to carry on. That is why this book doesn't ask you to pick a good week. It asks you to finish reading, and then stop, whatever week it is.

The book of Ecclesiastes has a line for the man who waits for perfect weather: "He who observes the wind won't sow; and he who regards the clouds won't reap."

## Three questions about when {-}

1. The first time you did it, as a boy, did you decide you'd go on doing it for life, with no way of stopping? Of course you didn't.
2. Are you going to keep it up until you die? Will you be at it at sixty, and at seventy-five, a grandfather waiting for the house to empty? Of course you aren't.
3. Then when will you stop?

Tomorrow? After finals? Next year? When you're married? Haven't you been asking that question since the day you first realized you couldn't leave it alone?

Perhaps you're hoping to wake up one morning and find you've simply lost interest in it. Stop kidding yourself. The path across the lawn gets more worn each year you walk it. It doesn't grow over while you're still using it. Or are you waiting until it has cost you something you can't get back? A marriage, say, or a calling, or the best ten years of your working life? That would be a strange time to choose.

Your life may be hard, and nobody here will tell you it isn't. But notice what the habit does to a hard life. It drains you every night and tells you every morning that you can't keep your own word. Hard work and long hours don't break men. What breaks them is the false crutch they lean on to get through.

## It won't be easier next year {-}

So look at it squarely. You've already decided you're not staying in this trap for life. That means that at some point, easy or hard, you'll go through the business of getting free. It won't be easier next year. It will be the same job with another year of rut worn in. So the time is now, or as soon after now as finishing this book allows.

Think how fast a week goes. Think of the rest of your life with no locked door, no secret and nothing to confess for the hundredth time. And if you follow the instructions, you won't be gritting your teeth through the first weeks, waiting for it to get better. You can find it easy, and even enjoy it.

Paul wrote to the church at Corinth, "Behold, now is the acceptable time." He was right. Keep reading.
